notes: Four developed sections, 40 workbook items, Pensa 8/8/8; no audio and no brevity or exercise exceptions. Demonstrative choices track real speaker viewpoint, the photographs and visible buildings.

First photo contains four young adults and four books beneath a large window, as in chapters 7–9; Ada and Marco identify the former room without disclosing the protected letter or the two unknown names. Second photo is a different view of that same room without people; no second real room is invented.

Mostrare is promoted at planned chapter 12; retain first reading 9, its existing sense identity, and add the first productive card now. Open slots: fotografia is receptive, while svuotare and spatial là are productive. Fotografia retains its planned productive date 31; no production answer/card uses it here. Mostrare is explicitly promoted with receptive_only false. Former-library identification and active furniture removal deliver the planned consequence and hook without passive or past-tense grammar.

Family citations/cards map singular and plural explicitly, instead of assigning all meanings to one surface. Fotografia is reading support for the planned title/photograph comparison; productive teaching stays at 31. No exercise/card requires its production. Each local demonstrative answer has a preceding prose demonstration; viewpoint is supported by qui/là and named holders.

Primary references checked for demonstrative viewpoint and adjective placement: Treccani aggettivi-e-pronomi-dimostrativi (Enciclopedia dell’Italiano) and aggettivi-qualificativi (La grammatica italiana). Original prose and examples; no quotation or external lexical dataset.

Nine delivered SVGs: one cover, two inline scenes, four vignettes and two margin diagrams. The first photograph reuses the published chapter-8 four people/books/window; new architectural detail aids do not alter earlier files. The historical chair in the second photo has no modern repair clamp. The prose supplies all referents without art. Lexical-date warnings distinguish actual reading from planned productive teaching; continuity is merged by finalize.

Review 1105-004507-5224 corrections: absence uses senza persone/non vedo persone; room emptying stays ongoing; the first photo’s evidence is people/books, not an absent table. The le gap reveals one letter. The combined B pool removes porta and adds three taught verb extras (bevo, abito, dovete); all substitutions are audited. Form-specific and inherited popup meanings are corrected. Pointing/sightline, last-item wording, varied stessi retrieval and the primo introduction ledger are aligned.

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: questa foto qui / quella foto lontano; la stessa stanza, due foto diverse.
grammar.note_en:
Demonstratives point to an identifiable person or thing. Questo means “this”, usually near the speaker, and quello “that”, farther away in the scene. They can also distinguish things being discussed: the characters point between two photographs on a table. Their forms follow the gender and number of the Italian noun. In the short rule, questa foto qui / quella foto lontano means “this photo here / that photo farther away”; la stessa stanza, due foto diverse means “the same room, two different photos”.

With a noun, questo has four main forms: questo pezzo, “this piece”; questa foto, “this photo”; questi fogli, “these sheets”; queste fotografie, “these photographs”. Foto is feminine and does not change in the plural; the demonstrative shows the difference. Fotografia is the full word: one fotografia, two fotografie, “one photograph, two photographs”.

Before a noun, quello changes its ending in a pattern like the definite article already learned. Quel pezzo is “that piece”; quella foto is “that photo”; quell’edificio is “that building”; quello scaffale is “that shelving unit”. In the plural, quei libri is “those books”, quelle finestre “those windows”, quegli scaffali “those shelving units” and quelle fotografie “those photographs”. The apostrophe in quell’edificio belongs to the shortened demonstrative before a vowel, not to the building noun. When the noun is left understood, the masculine forms are quello and quelli: il libro qui / quello lontano, “the book here / the one farther away”; i libri qui / quelli là, “the books here / the ones farther away”. Do not use quei on its own in that pattern.

Stesso means “the same”: la stessa finestra, “the same window”, refers to one window shown in both photographs. Uguale means “alike/equal” in the respect being compared; two different shelves can look alike without being one shelf. Diverso means “different”. The photos are different photographs of the same room. Altro means “other/another”, as in un altro posto, “another place”. The words are not interchangeable proofs of identity.

Descriptive adjectives often follow the noun, as in fotografie diverse, “different photographs”, and la biblioteca nuova, “the new library”. Some familiar adjectives also naturally precede the noun. La vecchia biblioteca means “the former library” here: it names Ada’s earlier library, rather than simply measuring the building’s age. La stessa finestra, “the same window”, and il primo dettaglio, “the first detail”, place their specifying adjectives before the noun. L’ultimo scaffale means “the last shelving unit”. Primo, secondo and ultimo mean “first”, “second” and “last” in a sequence; their endings agree with the noun, as in prima foto and seconda foto, “first photo” and “second photo”. These are examples of placement in this chapter, not a rule that every adjective can move freely.

Riconoscere means “recognize”: Ada sees features and identifies a place she remembers. Mostrare means “show”: Ada makes a detail available for Elena to see. Svuotare means “empty/remove the contents”: people carry furniture and books outside. The story uses active present verbs to show this action, without introducing a passive or a new past tense.

Là means “there”, pointing to the farther position; qui means “here”. Keep là, with its accent, distinct from the article or object form la. In the tables, Quelle sono le finestre means “Those are the windows”; the windows are farther away from the speaker.
